title: Developer Training & Technical Mentorship Program
description: I created and ran a structured Java training and onboarding program for every new developer hire joining my team. The course ran for roughly two to three months at a few hours per week alongside normal project work, and combined core programming concepts with the architecture, conventions, and expectations of our production codebase. New hires implemented data structures, sorting algorithms, design patterns, database mappings, and larger final projects before I considered them ready for deeper work in the main repository.

sections.title: Why I Created the Program
paragraphs: I created the course after repeatedly finding that academic credentials did not necessarily translate into strong production object-oriented programming or the ability to work safely inside an established codebase.

New hires could arrive from college or university with useful theoretical knowledge but still need substantial practice in code structure, architecture, maintainability, and the conventions required by our production software.
The goal was to bring every developer to a dependable common baseline before giving them deeper responsibility in the main code repository.

sections.title: Every New Developer Hire
paragraphs: Every new developer I hired went through the course, regardless of educational background.
It was intended specifically for new developer hires rather than co-op students because the curriculum was too substantial for short placements.
I can remember at least five developers completing the program.

sections.title: Two-to-Three-Month Onboarding
paragraphs: The course typically took about two to three months to complete.
It was not full-time training. Developers spent a few hours each week on the curriculum while continuing their normal day-to-day responsibilities.
The program evolved over the years as the production codebase and the needs of new hires changed.

sections.title: Pure Java Curriculum
paragraphs: The training was taught entirely in Java.
I explained each concept first, then required the developer to implement it themselves rather than only reading examples or discussing theory.

sections.title: Custom Data Structures
paragraphs: Developers implemented core data structures from scratch after learning the underlying concepts.

sections.title: Sorting Algorithms
paragraphs: Developers also implemented sorting algorithms directly so they understood the mechanics rather than treating library calls as black boxes.

sections.title: Design Patterns in Working Code
paragraphs: Design patterns were not taught only as definitions. Developers were required to use them in actual code.

sections.title: Object-Oriented Design
paragraphs: A major purpose of the course was improving practical object-oriented design and helping developers understand how to extend an existing architecture without fighting it.

sections.title: SQL and Java Entity Mapping
paragraphs: The curriculum included mapping relational SQL data into Java entities.
This helped developers understand the boundary between database structures and object-oriented application models.

sections.title: Learning the Production Codebase
paragraphs: A significant portion of the program was about our real production codebase, not generic programming exercises.
Developers learned the architecture, coding conventions, reusable systems, and expectations they would need when contributing to the main Essential Skills software.
I did not consider a new hire fully trusted for deeper repository work until they had completed the training.

sections.title: Final Project Choice
paragraphs: The course ended with a larger practical project that combined programming, architecture, UI, graphics, mathematics, and debugging.
Developers chose their own final project rather than having one assigned. The goal was practice and confidence-building, not a stress test.
Most developers chose the Particle Editor.

sections.title: Practice, Not a Stress Test
paragraphs: I deliberately let developers choose the final project because everyone needed the practice, but I did not want the onboarding process to become unnecessarily overwhelming.
The purpose was to get people productive and aligned with the team relatively quickly, not to eliminate candidates through artificial difficulty.

sections.title: Bidirectional Mentorship
paragraphs: Although I was responsible for training new hires in the production architecture and programming practices, the learning was not one-way.
Some developers brought expertise that I did not have and taught me areas such as SQL Server, stored procedures, and Windows 2000 setup.
I also encouraged developers to challenge or improve the engines and codebase because they were active users of the systems I was designing.

sections.title: Engineering Feedback Loop
paragraphs: New developers were not expected to silently conform to existing systems.
Once they understood the architecture, I listened to their feedback on the engines and codebase and used good ideas to improve the platform.
This made the onboarding process both a training mechanism and a practical feedback loop for the engineering organization.

sections.title: Long-Term Leadership Role
paragraphs: The program ran for many years as part of my management and engineering-lead responsibilities.

It helped standardize development practices across hires with very different educational and professional backgrounds while reducing the risk of inconsistent architectural decisions entering a large shared codebase.
